collection: Over water or upward delivery (since it is lighter than air and insoluble in water).
notes: Do not use alkali metals (too dangerous/explosive) or copper (no reaction).

equation: CH4 + H2O <-> CO + 3H2 | CO + H2O <-> CO2 + H2
collection: Pressure swing adsorption to purify the hydrogen.
notes: Endothermic process utilizing a Nickel catalyst at 700-1000°C, followed by the Water-Gas Shift reaction to maximize H2 yield.

collection: Over water.
notes: Manganese(IV) oxide acts as a catalyst and is not consumed in the reaction. This is often the safest lab method.

collection: Over water.
notes: Reactants must be heated. The MnO2 catalyst significantly lowers the decomposition temperature required.

collection: Over water.
notes: Requires strong heating. Potassium dichromate decomposes to yield oxygen gas alongside potassium chromate and chromium(III) oxide.

collection: Liquefaction followed by fractional distillation.
notes: Air is cooled to -200°C to liquefy it. Nitrogen boils off first at -196°C, leaving liquid oxygen which boils at -183°C.

equation: NH4Cl + NaNO2 -> NH4NO2 + NaCl | NH4NO2 -> N2 + 2H2O
collection: Over water.
notes: Direct heating of solid ammonium nitrite is explosive, so it is prepared safely in situ by heating an aqueous mixture of these two salts.

collection: Gas phase collection during fractional distillation.
notes: Air is liquefied, and N2 boils off first (-196°C) leaving O2 behind.

collection: Downward delivery (since it is heavier than air).
notes: Avoid using sulfuric acid as it forms an insoluble layer of calcium sulfate that stops the reaction.

collection: Gas extracted from rotary kilns.
notes: Thermal decomposition heated to ~900°C. Quicklime (CaO) is produced as a highly valuable primary product.

collection: Upward delivery (lighter than air). Cannot be collected over water as it is highly soluble.
notes: Reactants must be heated. The gas is dried using quicklime (CaO).

collection: Condensation of NH3 gas by cooling the equilibrium mixture.
notes: Uses an Iron catalyst at ~450°C and 200 atm pressure. It is a reversible, exothermic reaction.

collection: Downward delivery (heavier than air) in a fume cupboard.
notes: Requires gentle heating. Chlorine is highly toxic. It can be passed through water to remove HCl gas, and concentrated sulfuric acid to dry it.

collection: Collected at the anode.
notes: Electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution. NaOH and H2 are also produced as valuable byproducts.

collection: Downward delivery (heavier than air).
notes: Reaction occurs at room temperature. Heating further gives Na2SO4, but it forms a hard crust in lab glassware. Cannot be dried with ammonia.

collection: Dissolved in water to form Hydrochloric Acid.
notes: Highly exothermic. The reactant gases are often obtained cleanly as by-products from the Chlor-Alkali process.

collection: Downward delivery (heavier than air).
notes: Requires heating. Can also be prepared by reacting a sulfite (like Na2SO3) with dilute acid at room temperature.

collection: Downward delivery.
notes: Highly toxic with a rotten egg smell. Prepared on-demand using Kipp's Apparatus to control gas flow.

collection: Over water (as it readily reacts with oxygen in air).
notes: Nitric oxide is colorless but reacts instantly with air to form brown Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2).

collection: Downward delivery (heavier than air).
notes: NO2 is a toxic, heavy, brown gas. Alternately prepared by the thermal decomposition of Lead(II) Nitrate.

equation: S + O2 -> SO2 | 2SO2 + O2 <-> 2SO3 | SO3 + H2SO4 -> H2S2O7 | H2S2O7 + H2O -> 2H2SO4
collection: n/a
notes: Uses a Vanadium(V) oxide (V2O5) catalyst at ~450°C and 1-2 atm pressure.

collection: n/a
notes: Uses a Platinum-Rhodium catalyst at ~850°C.

collection: Aqueous solution extracted from cathode compartment.
notes: Electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution. Also produces valuable Cl2 and H2 gases.

collection: Used immediately in liquid form.
notes: Highly corrosive 3:1 molar ratio mixture. The active oxidizing agents are dissolved Cl2 and nitrosyl chloride (NOCl). It is capable of dissolving noble metals like Gold (Au) and Platinum (Pt).

collection: Downward delivery (heavier than air).
notes: This method is safer and more convenient than the copper-turnings approach as it proceeds at room temperature without requiring heating.

collection: Solid residue collected after heating.
notes: Requires strong heating in a crucible. CO2 gas is evolved. The product is quicklime, which reacts exothermically with water to form slaked lime Ca(OH)2.

collection: Solid iron collected from the reduction tube.
notes: A laboratory-scale demonstration of the blast furnace reduction. The iron produced is spongy and impure (containing slag).

equation: C + O2 -> CO2 | CO2 + C -> 2CO | Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2
collection: Molten iron tapped from the bottom of the furnace.
notes: Coke is combusted to produce CO2, which reacts with more coke to form CO (the reducing agent). Limestone (CaCO3) is added as a flux to remove impurities as slag (calcium silicate). The furnace operates continuously at temperatures up to ~2000°C.

collection: Sodium metal collected at the cathode, rising to the surface of the molten electrolyte.
notes: NaCl is mixed with CaCl2 to lower the melting point from ~801°C to ~600°C, saving energy. Sodium is highly reactive and must be stored under oil. Chlorine gas is collected at the anode.

collection: The solution is filtered to remove excess CuO, then crystallized to obtain blue CuSO4·5H2O crystals.
notes: CuO is a black powder that reacts with dilute H2SO4 upon heating to form a blue solution of copper(II) sulfate. Excess CuO ensures complete neutralization of the acid.

equation: NH3 + H2O + CO2 -> NH4HCO3 | NH4HCO3 + NaCl -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl | 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2
collection: Sodium carbonate is obtained by heating sodium bicarbonate.
notes: CO2 is obtained by calcining limestone. NH3 is recycled from NH4Cl by reacting it with Ca(OH)2 (from the lime kiln). This process is economical but produces CaCl2 as a waste byproduct.

collection: The mixture is distilled to obtain aqueous ethanol (~15% by fermentation alone, up to ~95% after distillation).
notes: Enzymes in yeast (zymase) catalyze the anaerobic breakdown of glucose. The process is carried out at ~30-35°C in the absence of air. Fractional distillation yields ethanol up to 95% purity; absolute ethanol requires drying agents.

collection: Condensed and purified by distillation.
notes: Uses a Phosphoric Acid (H3PO4) catalyst adsorbed on silica at ~300°C and ~60 atm. This direct hydration method produces high-purity ethanol and is the preferred industrial route.

collection: The solid slaked lime or its aqueous suspension (limewater) is collected.
notes: The reaction is highly exothermic and produces a white suspension of calcium hydroxide (milk of lime). The clear supernatant is limewater, used to test for CO2.

collection: The solution is filtered, then concentrated and crystallized to obtain pale green FeSO4·7H2O crystals.
notes: Hydrogen gas is evolved. Excess iron is used to prevent oxidation of Fe(II) to Fe(III). The crystals are efflorescent and easily oxidized; a small amount of dilute acid is added to the solution to stabilize it.

collection: The solution is filtered, concentrated by evaporation, and crystallized to obtain Pb(NO3)2 crystals.
notes: Lead(II) oxide is a yellow or red powder depending on the temperature at which it was prepared. Lead compounds are toxic and should be handled with care.

collection: The solution is evaporated and crystallized to obtain colorless AgNO3 crystals.
notes: Silver reacts only with nitric acid, not with dilute sulfuric or hydrochloric acid. Using concentrated HNO3 would produce NO instead of NO2. Silver nitrate is light-sensitive and must be stored in dark amber bottles.

collection: Molten sodium rises and is tapped off from the cathode region. Chlorine gas is collected separately at the anode.
notes: Industrial-scale electrolysis of molten NaCl at ~600°C in a Downs cell. A steel cathode and graphite anode are used, separated by a steel gauze diaphragm. CaCl2 is added to lower the melting point. Sodium is highly reactive and must be stored under mineral oil or in an inert atmosphere.

collection: Upward delivery (lighter than air). Cannot be collected over water as it is highly soluble.
notes: This is an alternative to the calcium hydroxide + ammonium chloride method. Sodium hydroxide is a stronger base, so the reaction proceeds readily with gentle heating. The gas should be dried using quicklime (CaO).
